NM-2026-HB107.s: The bill would change New Mexico's medical malpractice law, including some legal definitions and how claims are paid. It would lower a health care provider's personal liability limit to $200,000, keep limits on total damage awards in malpractice cases, and make payments from the patient's compensation fund as expenses are actually incurred. It would also limit punitive damages and attorney fees in malpractice claims.

NM-2026-HB110.s: Beginning July 1, 2026, certain New Mexico counties and cities would have to post quarterly housing development reports on their websites. The reports would cover residential land use and building permit applications, approval or denial status, processing times, staff levels, and could include short notes to explain the data. The rule would apply to class A counties and municipalities with more than 30,000 people.

NM-2026-HB190.s: The bill would set aside $1 million from the general fund for the Workforce Solutions Department to spend in fiscal year 2027. The money would support lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and queer people who are experiencing homelessness with eviction prevention and housing help. Any money left over at the end of fiscal year 2027 would go back to the general fund.

NM-2026-HB195.s: The bill would stop people from collecting a medical malpractice court order to pay from an independent provider’s personal income or personal property in most cases. It would cover certain licensed health workers, like doctors, nurse practitioners, and physician assistants, if a court finds they kept required malpractice coverage or had at least $1 million in insurance per claim. It would apply to medical malpractice claims brought after the bill’s effective date.

NM-2026-HB220.s: The bill would give counties more time before turning over some delinquent property tax cases to the Taxation and Revenue Department, changing the period from more than two years to more than four years. It would also raise the wait time before real property can be sold for unpaid taxes from three years to five years. These changes would affect county treasurers, the department, and property owners with unpaid property taxes.

NM-2026-HB278.s: The bill would set Medicaid payment rules for toxicology lab tests done by independent reference labs. It would require the state health agency to set billing codes and rules for these tests, based on medical need and clinical guidance, and it would allow the agency to check that a lab meets the program rules. The bill also sets aside $100,000 for fiscal year 2027 to carry out this payment system, and it would take effect on July 1, 2026.

NM-2026-HB289.s: The bill would change how New Mexico pays for school bus service for school districts and state-chartered charter schools. It would let transportation money cover the miles a bus travels to pick up the first student and to return after the last drop-off. It would also update how the state calculates each school’s transportation funding, with an effective date of July 1, 2026.

NM-2026-HB301.s: The bill would let the Department of Information Technology work on tech projects for courts and other parts of the judicial branch. It would also set up a yearly list of the tech goods and services the department can offer and the rates for them. The bill includes a $1.2 million state fund grant for the district attorneys' office to buy tech goods and services for district attorneys statewide.

NM-2026-HB320.s: The bill would create two programs in the Economic Development Department: one for production incentives and one for investment grants for New Mexico industrial facilities that cut carbon intensity. It would also require the Economic Development Department and the Department of Environment to set rules, set industry benchmarks, and use a new fund for these payments. The bill says incentives could pay $85 per ton of carbon dioxide reduced below the benchmark, and grants could cover 10% of qualified costs up to $5 million.

NM-2026-HB40.s: The bill would give retired members under the Educational Retirement Act a one-time extra payment each year in fiscal years 2027 and 2028. The payment would equal 2% of their annual annuity and would not be added into future payments. It would also set aside $65.5 million from the general fund to pay for these extra payments.

NM-2026-HB49.s: The bill would raise the penalty for a serious violent felon who receives, transports, or has a firearm or destructive device. For a first offense, the person would face a second-degree felony and at least nine years in prison. For later offenses, the charge would be a first-degree felony.

NM-2026-HB83.s: The bill would require the state health care authority to set minimum Medicaid pay rates for personal care services. It would also require personal care services agencies to spend at least 70% of that Medicaid money on direct care worker costs like pay, benefits, and training, and keep records to show it. The bill includes a $51.4 million general fund appropriation for fiscal year 2027 to update the fee schedule and raise these payments.

NM-2026-HJM1.s: This memorial would have the New Mexico Legislature support closer ties with Taiwan in trade, technology, education, official visits, and work with international groups. It also would encourage state agencies, colleges, and lawmakers to work with Taiwan on artificial intelligence, research, job training, student exchanges, and joint innovation. The memorial would also call for a New Mexico-Taiwan friendship caucus to help keep that work moving.

NM-2026-HJR1.s: This joint resolution would ask voters to amend the state constitution on board of regents appointments for state schools. It would set up nominating committees to send governor a list of names for nonstudent regents, and student regents would come from a list made by an elected student group. It would also require most regents to avoid changing party registration in the 12 months before appointment. The proposal would go to voters at the next general election or an earlier special election.

NM-2026-HM43.s: The memorial would ask the Legislative Education Study Committee and the Public Education Department to study how public school rankings are made in New Mexico and nearby states. It would look at student reading scores, called Lexile scores, and compare data such as math and reading achievement, graduation and dropout rates, funding, school safety, class sizes, and teacher credentials. The study findings and recommendations would go to the New Mexico Legislative Council by November 1, 2026.

NM-2026-SB103.s: The bill would update New Mexico’s aircraft law to treat directing a laser at a flying aircraft, along with firing a gun or launching an object at it, as unlawful interference. It would make a first offense a fourth-degree felony, with stronger penalties for later offenses or if someone on the aircraft needs medical treatment. It would also define the word "laser" in the law and repeal one older section on this topic.

NM-2026-SB106.s: The bill would give $5 million from the general fund to the Higher Education Department for fiscal year 2027 to carry out the Graduate Scholarship Act. It would affect the department and the graduate scholarship program it runs.

NM-2026-SB11.s: The bill would create a state loan repayment program for licensed nurses who work in New Mexico. It would help nurses in areas with too few nurses, and it would also cover some nursing faculty and student preceptors. The bill would create a fund and set aside $5 million for it, starting in fiscal year 2027.

NM-2026-SB112.s: The bill would change the types of investments allowed for New Mexico’s severance tax permanent fund. It would limit some “differential rate” investments, which are special investments meant to help the state economy, and clarify that other investments are “market rate” investments. It would affect how state fund managers invest money in the fund.

NM-2026-SB146.s: This bill would change New Mexico’s civil rights law for claims against public bodies, which include state and local government bodies and some related groups. It would set new damage limits, bar punitive damages, shorten the time to file a claim from three years to two, and require written notice within 90 days in most cases. It would also say a person cannot collect damages under both this law and the Tort Claims Act for the same event.

NM-2026-SB149.s: The bill would change the property tax code definition of "residential property." It would cover manufactured homes and other structures used mainly as homes, even if they are leased or rented to lodgers for any length of time. It would not treat hotels, motels, and similar commercial buildings as residential property.

NM-2026-SB15.s: The bill would require many New Mexico health plans and insurers to cover any type of health care provider when that provider is working within their legal scope of practice. It would apply to individual and group plans, health maintenance organization contracts, and nonprofit health care plans. It would take effect for plans and contracts entered into, renewed, extended, amended, or issued on or after July 1, 2026.

NM-2026-SB16.s: The bill would stop health care entities from directing a health care provider’s professional judgment or clinical choices, except when licensing or accreditation rules require it. It would also let a person who was harmed sue in court, and it would allow the attorney general to bring an enforcement case for the state. Courts could award damages, punitive damages, injunctions, costs, and attorney fees. The act would take effect July 1, 2026.

NM-2026-SB162.s: Regional housing authorities in New Mexico could form nonprofit groups to make support deals with the U.S. Department of Defense and its service branches. Those groups could work on leasing, building, fixing, or managing property inside or outside New Mexico. Money from those activities would go to affordable housing goals of the housing authority that created the nonprofit.

NM-2026-SB169.s: The bill would change how some retired public employees get cost-of-living raises. It would give a 1.68% raise on July 1, 2026 to certain retired members age 65 or older, and it would keep other raise rules for some long-term retirees, disability retirees, and older retirees. It would also set aside $10 million from the general fund for the retirement agency to pay for this in fiscal years 2027 and 2028.

NM-2026-SB204.s: The bill would give $100 million from the state general fund to the Higher Education Department for fiscal years 2027 and 2028. The money would help cover reduced or ended federal funding for existing research projects at the University of New Mexico, New Mexico State University, and the New Mexico Institute of Mining and Technology. It would apply to projects that could still be finished if the funding gap were filled.

NM-2026-SB219.s: The bill would create a new state office to help Native Americans in New Mexico by looking into concerns, trying to resolve them, and reporting on common problems. It would require people who serve Native Americans to post notice about the office, keep its records private, and bar retaliation against anyone who brings a concern. The bill would set aside $2 million from the general fund for the office and say it would take effect right away.

NM-2026-SB222.s: The bill would give $20 million from the general fund to the Health Care Authority for fiscal years 2027 through 2029. The money would be used to create new physician residency programs and residency positions, which train doctors after medical school.

NM-2026-SB228.s: The bill would set the state budget for fiscal year 2027 and give money to state agencies, courts, and other parts of state government. It also sets rules for how the money would be spent, including when unused funds must return to the general fund. The bill covers many agencies and programs, including the legislative, judicial, and district courts.

NM-2026-SB233.s: The bill would require New Mexico public schools to find 4th through 8th graders with math or reading scores in the bottom quartile and offer them high-impact tutoring. Schools would have to start tutoring within 30 days, use a trained tutor, keep groups to no more than four students per tutor, and provide it at least three times a week for at least 10 weeks. Parents would get notice, a written plan, progress reports, and guidance to help at home.

NM-2026-SB246.s: The bill would add licensing rules for massage therapy businesses and define a massage therapy establishment as a place where massage therapy is offered or done. It would let the board set standards, inspect these places, and fine or discipline people who run or work in an unlicensed place. It would also require new or renewed massage therapy licenses or registrations issued on or after July 1, 2026 to include a current photo.

NM-2026-SB250.s: This bill would require people convicted of driving on a revoked license to get an ignition interlock device, which is a breath test linked to a car, and to get an ignition interlock license within 10 days. It would also make that offense a court-of-record case in metropolitan court, set ignition interlock licenses at 4 or 8 years, and let an approved installer remove the device without a court order. The bill would also change the interlock device fund rules and raise some payment limits for device costs.

NM-2026-SB254.s: The bill would set aside $2.8 million from the general fund for the Department of Information Technology. The money would pay subscriber fees for the state’s digital trunked radio communications system for city, county, and tribal public safety agencies that handle police, fire, medical, or other emergency work. The funds would be available in fiscal year 2027 and later years, and unused money would stay available instead of going back to the general fund.

NM-2026-SB283.s: The bill would expand New Mexico’s metropolitan redevelopment rules to include housing shortage areas. It would let local governments use these rules for more redevelopment projects and define housing shortage areas as places with too little affordable housing, high costs, low vacancy, or not enough multifamily or workforce housing. It would also exempt a qualifying multifamily property in a housing shortage area from property tax for up to 20 years.

NM-2026-SB289.s: This bill relates to the public peace, health, safety, and welfare. It does not say in the official text what specific changes it would make or who would be affected.

NM-2026-SB313.s: The bill would let a court treat a child's failure to use a car seat, booster seat, or seat belt as fault or negligence in a crash case. It would remove the current rule that such a failure cannot reduce or split damages. This would affect children riding in passenger cars, vans, and pickup trucks, and the people involved in injury claims after a crash.

NM-2026-SB33.s: The bill would let people with life-threatening or severely debilitating illnesses try a custom investigational treatment made for them based on their genetic profile. It would let a manufacturer offer the treatment at a health facility, and a patient could ask for it with written, informed consent; the manufacturer could give it for free or charge the patient for the cost. The bill would also bar state officials from blocking access, protect health care providers from discipline for making such a recommendation, and say heirs would not owe debt for the treatment if the patient dies.

NM-2026-SB34.s: The bill would require the Public Education Department to report and publish data on standards-based test results from the prior school year by September 1 each year. The report would include pass rates by subject, grade, school, district, the state, and student groups, while protecting student privacy. It would also keep other school accountability reports, graduation data, and spending information in the department’s reporting system.

NM-2026-SB49.s: The bill would create a three-year pilot project in the Public Education Department for schools and charter schools to use a rating system for library materials based on age appropriateness. Selected participants would share rated book lists with parents, gather parent feedback, and give parents a survey about the system. It would give each participant two $25,000 grants and set aside $3,210,000 for the project from fiscal years 2027 through 2029.

NM-2026-SB52.s: The bill would change cost-of-living raises for certain public employee retirees and survivor beneficiaries in the Public Employees Retirement Act. Starting in 2027, their yearly pension increase would match the Social Security and Supplemental Security Income cost-of-living change for that year. It would also set aside $50 million from the general fund for these raises, and the act would take effect on December 1, 2026.

NM-2026-SB89.s: The bill would create a gross receipts tax break for some sales of hunting, fishing, camping, and firearm items each year from September 8 through December 31. It would cover certain low-priced fishing and camping gear, as well as ammunition, firearms, bows, crossbows, and some related accessories. Sales by businesses that operate under a franchise agreement would not qualify. The bill would take effect on July 1, 2026.

NM-2026-SJM1.s: This memorial would urge the U.S. Congress to pass a law that sets the same redistricting rules for congressional districts across states. It would also ask Congress to ban midcycle redistricting, unless a court orders it. The memorial would affect how congressional seats are drawn, but it would not change state law by itself.

NM-2026-SJR5.s: The resolution would ask voters to approve a change to the New Mexico Constitution on property taxes. It would let the Legislature limit yearly increases in the value of nonresidential property for tax purposes, with rules that could apply statewide or in some local areas. The change would go to the voters at the next general election or an earlier special election.

NM-2026-SM26.s: This memorial would ask the New Mexico Senate to support utilities joining regional power markets, including voluntary energy markets. It says this could help coordinate electric service across states, improve reliability, and keep power more affordable for residents. It also calls for oversight by the Public Regulation Commission and sends copies to state leaders and agencies.

NM-2026-SM28.s: This memorial would request the crime victims reparation commission to convene a statewide crime prevention task force to study firearms violence in New Mexico and make recommendations. The task force would include representatives from state agencies, law enforcement, Indian nations, tribes and pueblos, gun advocates and distributors, and anti-domestic violence and sexual assault groups. It would study the causes of firearms violence, review state and federal laws on gun ownership, possession and use, and report its findings to legislative committees and the governor.

NM-2026-SM7.s: This memorial would ask the New Mexico Legislative Council to form a redistricting task force to study ways to improve how district maps are drawn. The task force would look at changes to the state's redistricting law, how other states do it, and other possible reforms. It would include lawmakers, party leaders, and members of the public, and it would present its findings and ideas by December 31, 2027.
